parts.title: Sentence comprehension: Allotment note
parts.instructions: Read the short email from a friend. Choose the best word for each gap (1-5).
parts.passage:
Hi Mateo,

I wanted to tell you how our new neighbourhood garden plot is doing. Even though the soil looked quite dry at first, we soon [1] out how to improve it by mixing in homemade compost. Our plot coordinator, Fiona, always reminds us to [2] an eye on the young tomato plants whenever the weather turns windy. Next Saturday we are planning to build a wooden frame for climbing beans, [3] should give us much more space on the ground. You do not need to bring any heavy tools because the society [4] spades, watering cans, and gloves for everyone. Let me know if you would like to drop [5] this weekend to pick up some fresh lettuce!

Best,
Clara

questions.explanation: 'Worked out how to improve it' is the phrasal verb meaning figured out; 'made out' and 'looked out' do not fit here.
'Keep an eye on' is a fixed idiom meaning to watch or check something regularly.
'Which' introduces a non-defining relative clause after a comma, referring to the whole idea of building a wooden frame.
'Supplies ... for everyone' means provides tools for people to use; 'contains' and 'includes' describe what is inside something rather than offering it.
'Drop by' is a phrasal verb meaning to visit someone or a place briefly and informally.

parts.title: Text cohesion: Planting balcony tomatoes
parts.instructions: The first sentence of the text is in the right place. Put the five sentences (A-E) into the correct order (gaps 1-5) to make a clear story.
parts.passage: Last April, I decided to grow cherry tomatoes on my small city balcony for the very first time. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]
sentences: By late July, dozens of bright red tomatoes were hanging from the branches, ready to be picked for dinner.
First, I bought two deep plastic pots and filled them with rich organic soil from the local market.
However, after two weeks of warm sunshine, the stems grew so tall that they began to lean over in the breeze.
Once the soil was ready, I planted three tiny green seedlings and watered them gently every morning.
To solve that problem, I tied each main stem loosely to a bamboo stick so the plants could stand upright.

gaps.explanation: 'First, I bought two deep plastic pots...' starts the sequence by preparing the containers and soil.
'Once the soil was ready' refers directly to filling the pots with soil in the previous sentence and describes planting the seedlings.
'However, after two weeks of warm sunshine, the stems grew so tall...' introduces a problem with the growing seedlings.
'To solve that problem, I tied each main stem...' directly answers the leaning stems mentioned in the previous sentence.
'By late July, dozens of bright red tomatoes...' brings the growing season to a successful harvest at the end of the story.

parts.title: Opinion matching: Community food gardens
parts.instructions: Four people (A-D) give their opinions about urban community gardens and growing fresh vegetables. Match each statement (1-7) to the correct person. You can use each person more than once.

texts.title: Dev
texts.text: People often tell me that growing vegetables in a city plot saves them a fortune at the supermarket, though I have not found that to be true. Once you pay for annual plot rent, seeds, and compost, a basket of courgettes costs roughly the same as it does at the market. What makes the garden priceless for me is the flavour. Picking crisp peas straight off the plant and eating them within an hour is something no shop can offer.

texts.title: Hannah
texts.text: I joined our local allotment three years ago mainly because I wanted fresh salads without plastic packaging. To my surprise, the social side has become even more important than the harvest. Every Sunday morning, neighbours swap spare seedlings, share recipes for leftover pumpkins, and look after each other's beds during holidays. My only frustration is that the waiting list for new plots is now over two years long.

texts.title: Liam
texts.text: When I first rented a small raised bed near my flat, I spent far too much money on fancy tools and exotic seeds that never grew well in our cool climate. Now I stick to hardy crops like kale, onions, and carrots, and my grocery bill has dropped noticeably since May. I also love that my young son helps me water the beds after school instead of staring at a tablet.

texts.title: Tessa
texts.text: I volunteer at a rooftop garden above a busy office block, where most of our harvest goes straight to a neighbourhood food bank. Unlike private allotments where everyone works alone on their own patch, we plant and harvest everything together as a team. I used to worry that air pollution in the city centre would spoil the leaves, yet regular soil tests show our vegetables are completely clean and safe to eat.

parts.title: Long text comprehension: Growing food in the city
parts.instructions: Read the article about urban community gardens and city food growing. Match each paragraph (1-7) to the best heading (A-H). There is one extra heading that you do not need.

paragraphs.text: Walk behind a row of tall brick flats in almost any large city today, and you might find a surprising patch of green. Empty corners beside railway lines, concrete yards behind schools, and flat roofs above supermarkets are being turned into neat wooden beds filled with spinach, beans, and herbs. As city populations grow and supermarkets rely on long lorry journeys, many residents are looking for ways to produce fresh food closer to home. Even a small strip of soil can supply dozens of families with crisp greens throughout the summer.

This idea is not completely new. During the nineteenth century, rapidly growing industrial towns left factory workers in crowded streets with little outdoor space and limited access to affordable vegetables. Local authorities and charities began dividing fields on the edge of towns into small rented plots, known as allotments. Families used these plots not as flower gardens, but as practical food sources where they grew potatoes, cabbages, and onions to feed their children through hard winters.

Growing vegetables in a modern city brings several practical challenges that countryside farmers rarely face. Urban soil near old roads or former workshops sometimes contains traces of paint or metal, so gardeners often build raised wooden boxes and fill them with clean soil brought from outside. Watering can also be tricky in summer when there is no river nearby. Many community sites therefore fix large barrels under shed roofs to collect free rainwater whenever a storm passes.

Beyond filling dinner plates, shared gardens quietly change the way neighbours treat one another. In busy cities where people often ride the same lift without saying hello, watering cans and seed packets give strangers an easy reason to start talking. Retired gardeners teach younger tenants how to prune tomato vines, while newcomers share herbs and cooking tips from their home countries. Over a single season, a quiet piece of grass often turns into a lively meeting place.

Local schools have also noticed how strongly outdoor food projects engage young learners. Instead of reading about plant life only in science textbooks, pupils measure how quickly radishes sprout, count bees on bean flowers, and taste fresh carrots they pulled from the ground themselves. Teachers report that children who normally refuse green vegetables in the school canteen are far more willing to eat a salad when they have watered and harvested the leaves with their own hands.

Urban food plots do more than support people; they also create safe islands for city wildlife. Even a narrow row of runner beans, flowering herbs, and berry bushes offers nectar and shelter for bees, butterflies, and small garden birds. Because community gardeners usually avoid harsh chemical sprays on food they plan to eat, helpful insects such as ladybirds thrive naturally and keep harmful pests under control without damaging the surrounding environment.

Despite their clear benefits, many urban gardens face an uncertain future because land in city centres is expensive. When a council or private owner decides to build new flats or offices, temporary garden plots are often the first spaces to disappear. To protect them, local volunteers increasingly form official societies, sign long-term leases, and invite town planners to see how much value these green corners bring to public health and neighbourhood life.

headings: How historical food plots helped industrial towns
Protecting city gardens from future building plans
Why supermarket vegetables are cheaper than homegrown ones
Turning unused urban corners into food spaces
Helping children enjoy science and healthy eating
Bringing diverse neighbours together through shared work
Practical solutions for soil and water in towns
Creating chemical-free homes for insects and birds

gaps.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes empty corners, concrete yards, and flat roofs being turned into wooden beds for growing vegetables in the city.
Paragraph 2 explains the nineteenth-century origin of allotments in industrial towns to help factory workers grow food.
Paragraph 3 details city-specific problems with contaminated soil and lack of water, and solutions like raised boxes and rainwater barrels.
Paragraph 4 focuses on how shared gardens help strangers talk, swap tips across generations and cultures, and build community.
Paragraph 5 explains how school food projects help pupils learn science practically and become more willing to eat vegetables.
Paragraph 6 describes how chemical-free urban plots provide nectar and shelter for bees, butterflies, ladybirds, and birds.
Paragraph 7 explains the threat of new buildings replacing temporary plots and how volunteers sign long-term leases to protect them.

task.title: Greenleaf Allotment Society — Watering and fee update

sourceEmail.subject: Temporary water pipe shut-off and annual plot fee change
sourceEmail.body:
Dear Members,

The city water company is repairing the main pipe along Oak Street, so our outdoor taps will be turned off for the next three weeks. During this period, members will need to carry water in containers from the park fountain two streets away. In addition, the annual plot fee will rise by £15 next season to cover new compost bins and tool repairs.

Please write to us if you have any questions or practical ideas.

Kind regards,
Fiona Reid
Plot Coordinator

task.prompt:
Write BOTH emails clearly labelled:

1. Informal email to a friend who shares a plot with you (40-50 words): say how you feel about the water shut-off and fee rise, and suggest how you can both manage watering.

2. Formal email to the plot coordinator, Fiona Reid (120-150 words): explain your concerns about carrying water and the higher fee, and suggest a practical solution for the society.

parts.title: Information matching: City vegetable plots

turns.speaker: spA

turns.speaker: spB

turns.speaker: spC
turns.text: Speaker C: My eight-year-old daughter used to push every green vegetable to the side of her plate. Since we started sharing a plot near her school, she checks our bean plants every afternoon and proudly washes the carrots she pulled herself. Seeing where food actually comes from has made her much more curious about trying healthy meals.

turns.speaker: spD
turns.text: Speaker D: People think I grow potatoes to save money, though seeds and tools add up! For me, the best part is cutting down on waste. At the allotment, I pick only the exact handful of leaves I need for dinner, zero plastic bags are involved, and every peel goes straight back into our shared compost heap.

parts.title: Monologue comprehension
parts.instructions: Listen to two speakers giving short talks: first a garden manager about a rooftop farm (questions 1-2), then a chef about cooking with urban-grown herbs (questions 3-4). Choose the best answer for each question.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: First, you will hear Dev, a project manager, talking about turning a supermarket roof into a vegetable garden.

turns.speaker: dev
turns.text: When our team first proposed planting vegetables on top of a city supermarket, everyone assumed our biggest headache would be carrying heavy soil bags up four flights of stairs. Actually, the building had a wide goods lift, so moving soil took just one weekend. The real surprise came during our first windy April. Up on the fourth-floor roof, strong gusts snapped young bean stems almost overnight until we built low wooden windbreaks around every bed. We originally planned to sell all our salads directly inside the supermarket downstairs. However, customers kept stopping us at the lift to ask how we grew tomatoes in shallow trays, so we started running free Saturday tours instead. Seeing office workers leave with a bunch of mint and plans for their own balcony pots has become the most satisfying part of my week.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Now you will hear Nora, a neighbourhood cafe cook, talking about using herbs from a nearby community plot.

turns.speaker: clara
turns.text: Three years ago, our cafe used to order plastic boxes of basil, coriander, and parsley from a wholesale supplier forty miles away. Even when they arrived on Monday morning, half the leaves were already bruised or yellowing by Thursday. When a group of neighbours started growing herbs in wooden boxes two streets from our kitchen, I asked if we could buy whatever extra bunches they harvested. Working with community growers means I never know on Sunday night exactly which herbs will arrive on Tuesday morning, so I have to write flexible daily specials rather than fixed printed menus. Some chefs hate that uncertainty, yet it keeps cooking exciting! If any cafe owner wants to partner with an urban garden, my main tip is to agree on a simple weekly delivery time and pay promptly, because volunteers fit garden work around full-time jobs.

parts.instructions: Look at the two photographs. First describe and compare them (45 seconds), then answer the two numbered questions (45 seconds each).
parts.prompt:
Tell me what you see in these two photographs and compare the two ways of enjoying fresh vegetables. Then answer these two questions:
1. What are the advantages of buying vegetables at an outdoor farmers' market compared with preparing freshly harvested vegetables at home?
2. Which of these two activities would you prefer to do on a Saturday morning, and why?

parts.title: Personal experience and discussion
parts.instructions: You have 1 minute to prepare and 2 minutes to speak continuously. Answer all three questions in one organised talk.

topics.prompt:
Talk about a time when you worked outdoors or helped grow or prepare food with other people. Answer all three questions in one 2-minute talk:
1. Tell me about a time when you worked outdoors or prepared fresh food with others.
2. How did you feel while you were doing this activity?
3. Why do you think shared green spaces are important for people living in modern cities?
